title: Sariputta's calm
hookLine: the wise one's verses: I don't long for death, I don't long for life (Theragatha, Sariputta)
carry: as a servant waits for wages

cards: Payday. The work is already done. The money will come when it comes.
A worker who's finished doesn't stand at the door all week waiting for it, and doesn't forget about it either.

Sariputta, the disciple tradition remembers for his wisdom, reaches for that very picture in his verses: a hired worker, waiting for his wages. It's how he describes waiting for the end of his own life.

teach.h: NO LONGING FOR DEATH, NOR FOR LIFE.
teach.b: First, the two refusals. Sariputta says: I don't long for death. I don't long for life.
He isn't hurrying toward the end, and he isn't clutching at more time. Second, the picture.

teach.h: LIKE A WORKER WAITING FOR WAGES.
teach.b: I wait for my time, he says, as a servant waits for wages, and he adds something that matters: mindful, and clearly knowing. A hired worker who has finished the job isn't chasing the pay as a prize.
It's simply what comes next. Sariputta's work, the long training of the mind, is complete. What's left is to wait, awake, without leaning either way.

In his verses he says the teacher has been served, the heavy burden laid down, what leads to becoming rooted out. Other elders in the Theragatha close their songs with words like these. It's their way of saying: done.
Fourth, why this can unsettle a listener. A line that won't long for life can sound bleak at first. Read in his verses, it sounds closer to ease.

teach.h: AS A SERVANT WAITS FOR WAGES.
teach.b: He just isn't grasping in either direction. Some readers hear in it the end of fear. Others hear a craftsman's quiet pride in finished work.
Either way, the picture is plain: a worker at the end of the day, tools put away, sitting on the step until the pay arrives.

how: Theravada teachers sometimes recite Sariputta's lines about not longing for death or life when speaking of how a freed person meets the end, and they are read at some reflections on death.

o: a calm that comes from finishing every chore
waiting without longing for death or for life
the wise one's habit of never speaking

s: Sariputta says he longs for death
he says he longs for neither death nor life.
he pictures himself as a worker waiting for wages
the work is finished; what's left is to wait for his time.
in his verses the waiting is anxious
he waits mindful and clearly knowing.

games.q: you're Sariputta. the work of training the mind is done, and the end of your life lies ahead. how do you meet it?
o: hold on to life for as long as you can.
wait for it, as a worker waits for wages.
games.why: he longs for neither death nor life. he waits for his time, mindful and clearly knowing, like a hired worker waiting for his pay.

practice: Choose something you're waiting on, a reply, a result, a season of life to end or to begin, and hold it in mind, then let go of the handle, neither pulling it closer nor pushing it away.
Sit the way a worker sits when the work is done, not watching the door, and each time the mind leans toward the thing, lean back into the breath.

wordCard.voice: Sariputta's calm. The wise disciple's verses: no longing for death, no longing for life, waiting for his time, mindful, as a worker waits for wages. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: bhataka, a hired worker. Sariputta waits for his time as one waits for wages.

carryVoice: Your line: as a servant waits for wages. Not hurrying, not clutching, just awake. That's day eight hundred four.
